title: Extending digital networks (US$20.0 million)
evidence_text: The subcomponent will assist authorities in elaborating a competitive bidding process with capital subsidies for telecom operators, develop a PPP manual, and establish a future‑proofed open‑access governance model to address market failures in rural areas.
rationale: The description outlines a materially different institutional and financing arrangement (PPP‑based competitive tender with post‑completion subsidies, open‑access governance) that is not routine for Cameroon, indicating a potential innovation, though the text does not explicitly label it as such.

   project will focus on areas that meet criteria set out in the PIM, including (a) an overall lack of

   infrastructure and absence of future expansion plans by telecom and broadband operators; (b) an

   expected sizeable and unsatisfied demand for digital services; (c) the feasibility and safety of engaging in

   on-site interventions, considering the areas affected by civil unrest, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters,

   and climate change; and (d) a geographic overlap with the interventions of Component 3. Given the

   modification of the regulatory framework envisioned through Component 1, the conditions for

   investment will significantly evolve for private operators; as a result, an extensive mapping exercise will

   be required to precisely determine those areas of intervention, considering the new policies and

   regulations (for example, rules determining the ability of operators to lay down fiber, rules on the

   mutualization of infrastructure, and coverage obligations).



   35.      This subcomponent will include a TA, developed in close collaboration with telecom operators,

   internet service providers and local authorities, to map the availability and demand of digital

   infrastructure and services and identify areas subject to market failures. The TA will focus on gathering

   data related to the deployment of digital services in Cameroon and presenting them in a friendly manner

   to policymakers. This task will require strong coordination between the public stakeholders (ministries,

   state and local institutions, regulators, and CAMTEL) and the private sector. The produced digitalized maps

   will be hosted by the ART, and real-time access will be granted to MINPOSTEL and other public entities

   (for instance, with ministries in charge of transport and energy, to improve coordination in infrastructure

   roll-out) and the telecom operators, with proper access rights associated to each type of user. The maps

   will be constantly updated under the leadership of ART through regular and mandated information

   requests to all telecom infrastructure owners. The mapping will have enough breadth, accuracy, and

   granularity for the preparation of the technical specifications of the tenders to cover the areas of

   Cameroon that are targeted by the project (Subcomponent 2.1) and the entities and sites to which the

   project will bring connectivity (Subcomponent 2.2), and it will focus on:



      (a)   Infrastructure and service mapping. The current availability of the digital infrastructure and

            service availability, to be validated through consultations with the private sector;

      (b)   Demand mapping. The demand topology and quantification of digital services (voice and data) to

            address the needs of end users (rural farmers, female entrepreneurs, and local public

            administrations), considering gender gaps in access, affordability, and usage (to be realized in

            close partnership with local authorities); and

      (c)   Investment mapping. Mapping the existing and planned investments in digital infrastructure by

            the private and public sectors. This will highlight investments that would be made purely by the

            private sector under the new policies and regulations and thus make explicit to policymakers the

            impact of policies and regulations conducive to private investments in the sector.



   36.      This subcomponent will then assist the authorities in elaborating the detailed strategy to roll

   out digital connectivity through a competitive bidding process for areas where market failure is

   confirmed. The network rollout will target only the areas with evidence of market failure by awarding

   capital subsidies to telecom operators through a competitive bidding process. This approach will aim to

   select the most economically advantageous offers (that is, the combination of a reverse tender process

   that favors the bidder asking for the lowest amount of project funds and a standard tender process

The World Bank

Acceleration of the Digital Transformation of Cameroon Project (P173240)







   favoring the bidder achieving the best output) among telecom operators, which will be responsible for

   the installation, operation, and maintenance of the network access infrastructure on an open-access basis,

   in exchange for a capital subsidy66 paid after the works are completed and validated by a commission

   established to accept such works. It is expected that the strategy will define an approach with multiple,

   geographically-delimited public-private partnership (PPP) projects being tendered and then implemented

   in parallel. The TA will guide this effort by incorporating the following principles in the tendering process:



        (a)   Technological neutrality. The type of network access will be selected by the bidders, based on

              their own assessment of the most appropriate technology. 67 Quality requirements will be

              established, and retail service price caps set in accordance with regional benchmarks.

        (b)   Climate change resilience and adaptation. The impact of climate change will be incorporated in

              the design of technical solutions, for instance, to increase resilience to landslides and accelerated

              erosion and to ensure the sustainability of these solutions by preventing environmental

              degradation and reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (for example, the use of solar power

              or other renewable energy sources for active equipment and overall compliance with ‘Green ICT

              standards’68).

        (c)   Future-proofed governance. The chosen governance model, which will be developed in close

              collaboration with the private sector, will ensure that Cameroon sets up and implements a future-

              proofed governance mechanism for any contract(s) awarded, in which the open-access principle

              is fully enforced.

        (d)   Open and transparent tendering process. It is expected that bidders will be primarily national

              telecom network operators. However, specialist tower operators (towercos) may also bid to

              provide the passive infrastructure, and there may be scope for innovative technology models.69



   37.      In compliance with these principles, this subcomponent will assist the authorities in elaborating

   a ‘PPP Manual’ for the use of project funds, elaborating tender documents for the selection of

   operators, provide on-time Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) subsidies to selected operators and support

   the implementation phases. The PPP manual, which will be integrated into the Project Implementation

   Manual, will describe the major transaction cycles and fund flow processes in this component and will

   allow PPP projects to be launched. These processes would cover the authorization procedures for

   transactions, financial and accounting policies, budgeting procedures, financial forecasting procedures,

   procurement and contract administration monitoring procedures, and auditing arrangements. This TA will

   include the preparation of the relevant tender documents, which cover (a) the prioritization, mapping,

   and clustering of the targeted areas; (b) the access services to be offered and their corresponding service-

   level agreements; (c) the infrastructures that will be financed, as they relate to the telecom, power supply,

22. In Mauritania, the selected project activity is the rehabilitation of Nouakchott Fish

Market. The fish market, located in the capital city, is a major hub of regional seafood trade and

it provides jobs to about 5,000 to 8,000 workers daily. The project activities will include:

     (2) Fencing the entire perimeter of the site for security purposes;

     (4) Construction of warehouses and administrative buildings.



23. In Guinea, a potential investment concept has been identified in Koukoudé village in the

prefecture of Boffa. While the exact site location is not yet determined, the investment will aim

to expand or improve fish landing and market facilities to serve artisanal fishers supplying the

domestic market. Site selection has not been finalized partly because the ongoing Ebola

outbreak has prevented further field visits or studies. The proposed menu of investments for the

site includes: (a) landing platform with access ramps; (b) basic platform on which private sector

may investment in fish processing plant or unit, warehouse to store and repair equipment, and

cold room; (c) administrative offices; (d) sanitation works; (e) auction hall; (f) first aid room; and

(g) latrines. The project will support studies on potential environmental impacts and resettlement

of affected populations due to the investment.

title: Contingent Emergency Response Component (US$0.0 million)
evidence_text: "a Contingent Emergency Response Component (CERC) is added to the project structure to allow for quick disbursement of uncommitted balances as a crisis response measure... to allow for an agile and rapid reallocation of project funds"
rationale: The CERC introduces a financing/process mechanism for rapid fund reallocation during crises, which is not a routine component of World Bank projects. The text explicitly presents it as a new addition, indicating novelty, but similar mechanisms exist elsewhere, so the evidence supports a possible innovation rather than confirmed innovation.
text:
55.       In the context of a rapidly developing COVID-19 emergency, a Contingent Emergency Response

   Component (CERC) is added to the project structure to allow for quick disbursement of uncommitted

   balances as a crisis response measure for this COVID-19 situation or any future ones. This will have an

   initial zero value but may be financed during the implementation of the project to allow for an agile and

   rapid reallocation of project funds in the event of a natural or man-made crisis or emergency during

   project implementation to address EEs under conditions established in the PIM.



     C.      Project Beneficiaries



   56.     The project will benefit a wide range of beneficiaries, including end users in rural areas, public-

   sector entities and civil servants, the private sector, and the general population:

      (a)   End users of digital services in target areas. The proposed project targets areas where access to

            digital services and the adoption of broadband are lagging. Rural dwellers—including the youth,

            women, and people with disabilities—will benefit from access to affordable broadband internet

            and will be able to procure mobile handsets through subsidies and/or payment facilities. In

            addition, they will benefit from digital literacy training programs and will be able to access public

            services more efficiently through online platforms, as well as to consume online content and

            services tailored to rural communities. The project will also ensure equitable participation of

            marginalized or vulnerable groups in entrepreneurial activities and digital skills training programs

            by alleviating constraints such as financing, care, access, and transportation. Gender- and

            location-disaggregated data on connectivity will also be recorded to monitor and track progress

            on key parameters of digital inclusion.

      (b)   Public-sector entities in target areas. Public hospitals, health care centers, schools, universities,

            CTD, and agricultural centers will benefit from affordable broadband connectivity and quality

            internet access. In addition, entities that promote digital skills and entrepreneurship (for example,

            incubators, accelerators, coworking spaces, and technology parks) will benefit from improved

            connectivity and access, the acquisition of digital equipment, and capacity-building for their staff.

      (c)   Farmers. Selected smallholder farmers will receive input subsidies through E-vouchers. The target

            smallholder farmers include crop and non-crop farmers and pastoralists in the following strategic

            value chains for MINADER and MINEPIA: cassava, rice, coffee, cashew, fish, bovine milk, pork, and

The World Bank

Acceleration of the Digital Transformation of Cameroon Project (P173240)







            chicken. The targeted number of direct beneficiaries is approximately 35,125 smallholder farmers,

            livestock-rearing farmers, and pastoralists, out of which 20,099 are agricultural smallholder

            farmers and 15,026 are smallholder livestock-rearing farmers and pastoralists. A matching grant

            will also be provided to producer organizations, associations, cooperatives, and farmers to

            promote adoption of digital innovations developed by agritech startups.

      (d)   Startups and entrepreneurs. The most prominent agritech startups and entrepreneurs will be

            selected through an innovation challenge event and will be offered contracts that will enable

            them to expand their services.

      (e)   Governmental agencies and civil servants. MINPOSTEL, MINADER, MINEPIA, ART, and ANTIC will

            be able to procure critical equipment, and they will benefit from capacity building and digital skills

            training. The data-driven agriculture and information systems will strengthen the public policy-

            making tools at the national and regional levels. The enrolled officers in rural agricultural training

            and animation centers will also benefit from digitalization, training, and capacity building.

      (f)   Private market players in the digital and agritech sectors. Private businesses in the target areas

            will get access to broadband and a digitally savvy workforce, and digital market players will benefit

            from an improved business environment. The private agritech sector will also benefit from the

            organization of innovation challenges focused on agriculture, acceleration activities, contracts,

            and matching grants. The e-voucher for agricultural inputs will also support the development of

            digital finance in the country.

      (g)   General population. Nearly every current or future user of telecom and digital services will benefit

            from the legal and regulatory reforms aimed at reducing costs, improving service quality, and

            stimulating investment and innovation. At the macro level, the project will support increased

            economic growth, productivity, and job creation, both within the digital and agricultural sectors

            and through spillover effects on other productive sectors.



     D.      Results Chain



   57.     The table below presents the project’s results chain/theory of change and includes the

   following assumptions:

           (a) The GoC supports the reform of the telecom/broadband sector.

           (b) The Government’s investment in the sector encourages private-sector entry into the market.

           (c) The regulator can fulfill its duties independently, impartially, and effectively.

           (d) Broadband connectivity and cost are the main drivers of user demand.

           (e) Beneficiary farmers who are granted input subsidies through e-vouchers build stronger

                confidence in the use of digital tools for other agricultural activities.

           (f) Agritech entrepreneurs are sufficiently motivated to expand their services to rural farmers

                in remote regions.

     E.       Rationale for World Bank Involvement and Role of Partners



   58.      The World Bank brings long expertise in supporting similar digital projects globally, as well as

   local knowledge. The World Bank’s added value includes (a) technical expertise in enabling policy and

   regulatory frameworks in the telecom/broadband sector, including earlier work in Cameroon telecom and

   a digital economy country diagnostic under the DE4A initiative; (b) technical expertise around the design

   of the e-voucher scheme and the approaches used to scale up DATs and the digital innovation ecosystem

   for agricultural development; (c) the ability to use a range of products and services in support of public-

   and private-sector actors; and (d) the ability to generate more equitable and beneficial development

   outcomes. For example, the e-voucher mechanism has been proposed based on operational experiences

   in Nigeria and Uganda and the analysis of pilot experiences in Mali, Chad, Niger, and Guinea. 82 The

   proposed project will also emulate the proven approaches adopted by the World Bank’s Digital Agriculture

   Africa team (DAT-Africa team) in successfully scaling up digital innovation in agricultural programs through

   World Bank-financed investment projects.83 The World Bank has been supporting digital transformation





   82 AFCW3 Economic Update, Evidence from E-voucher programs in Mali, Niger, Chad and Guinea, Digitizing Agriculture, Spring

   2019, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/31576/Digitizing-Agriculture-Evidence-from-E-Voucher-

   programs-in-Mali-Chad-Niger-and-Guinea.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y.

   83 The DAT-Africa team organized innovation challenges in Kenya and Uganda to select agritech enterprises with demonstrably



   scalable models to address sector challenges of agricultural productivity, market links, financial inclusion, energy, and data

   analytics and agricultural intelligence. In both countries, the team is now working with ecosystem partners to deploy the

   selected enterprises through three ongoing World Bank-supported projects with aggregate investments of US$600 million that

The World Bank

Acceleration of the Digital Transformation of Cameroon Project (P173240)







   across six global regions for several decades and has been involved for a long time in Cameroon in both

   the telecom and agricultural sectors.



   59.     There is a strong rationale for the public financing of this project, given the public good nature

   of the benefits derived from the project across social and economic sectors and the potential to increase

   overall inclusion. The project will enable investments in digital connectivity in vital sectors such as

   agriculture, health, and education. In addition, the project will address inclusion concerns in terms of

   gender, disability, geography, and income levels to compensate for market failures and ensure that the

   most vulnerable are not excluded from the social and economic benefits of Cameroon’s digital

   transformation. Moreover, the improved internet connectivity and digital services that are made possible

   through public interventions can dramatically improve Cameroon’s resilience to shocks (for example,

   emergency calls, monitoring and tracking in dangerous areas, enabling digital communication, health

   diagnosis, and distance learning during health crises such as COVID-19).



   60.      Component 1 will seek to establish the conditions to incentivize private sector investment in

   digital services in line with the MFD approach, while Component 2 will finance infrastructure in areas

   where market failures prevent private-sector interventions in the absence of public-sector funding or

   de-risking. A significant improvement of the policy and regulatory environment appears necessary to

   unleash more private investment in the digital sector. Component 1 will aim to establish and perpetuate

   such an environment. In addition, given the lack of incentives for private telecom operators to extend

   digital services to areas and populations for which the financial return prospects are limited or negative,

   public sector co-funding is primordial. Digital services have increasingly become a necessity for

   households and yet remain out of reach for many segments of the population due to accessibility or

   affordability. Reducing this digital divide by increasing coverage, lowering prices, improving service

   quality, and providing mobile devices to the population—especially in underserved regions—can

   significantly close the opportunities gap between population segments.



   61.      Public funding of Component 3 is required given the challenges to scale up DATs in terms of

   capital needs, coordination among stakeholders, and access to data. The development of foundational

   data infrastructures and acceleration of digital agricultural technologies can enable the delivery of farm-

   level, geospatial, and real-time analytics to inform policies and targeted investments by governments,

   agribusinesses, and intermediary service providers. However, scaling up digital agricultural technologies

   involves generating and accessing large-scale national data sets, a costly challenge for any individual

   market player. Even when data sets are affordable, they are not accessible or shareable across silos, and

   private-sector players lack incentives to share private data sets with the broader ecosystem. Public

   interventions are thus needed, especially given that certain types of data have strong public goods

   components and rely on substantial up-front investments in data capture and analytics infrastructures

   that the private sector may be unwilling to subsidize. Public financing to support, enable, and develop the

   innovation ecosystem for digital agriculture also addresses classic coordination failures and offers longer-

   term sustainability returns for both the private sector as well as farmers.

   62.     Component 3 has potential synergies with the work and investments of the International

   Finance Corporation (IFC) in Cameroon. In line with this project and building on its current portfolio, IFC

   plans to step up support to the private agriculture sector, including tools such as rural finance, crop

   insurance, and warehouse receipts. The World Bank will build on this project along with IFC on future

   Advisory Services and Analytics to support private investment in agriculture. IFC will continue supporting

   agriculture finance, in particular through its investments in Banque Internationale du Cameroun pour

   l’Epargne et le Crédit (BICEC) and SFC Agri RSF (Risk Sharing Facility established by BICEC), which have

   been financing credit lines to farmers while strengthening value chains and competitiveness. Under

   Subcomponent 3.3, the World Bank will leverage IFC’s expertise to provide a matchmaking program

   (previously done through TechEmerge) that connects companies worldwide with leading organizations in

   emerging markets.



   63.      The project complements existing programs run by partner organizations that support

   agricultural development in Cameroon. The International Fund for Agricultural Development financed

   several activities with a similar focus on digital innovation and youth, including the Program for the

   Promotion of Agropastoral Youth Entrepreneurship, the Commodity Value Chain Support Project, and the

   Aquaculture Entrepreneurship Promotion Project. The African Development Bank is another potential

   partner for livestock and fish farming value chains (Livestock and Fish Farming Value Chains Development

   Project through the Agricultural Value Chain Development Project. Other partners include the French

   Development Agency (Agence Française de Développement, AFD), the Japan International Cooperation

   Agency (JICA), and the German International Cooperation Agency (Deutsche Gesellschaft für

   Internationale Zusammenarbeit, GIZ). AFD carried out a program for the development of vocational

   training in the agricultural, livestock, and fishing sectors and the Improvement of the Competitiveness of

   Agricultural Family Farming Program. JICA invests heavily in the rice sector through the Project for the

   Development of Irrigated and Rainfed Rice Cultivation, and GIZ operates the green innovation centers for

   the Agriculture and Food Sector project. The project could also collaborate with the ongoing World Bank-

   financed Rural Electricity Access Project for Underserved Regions (P163881) to increase productive uses

   of energy in agriculture.



     F.      Lessons Learned and Reflected in the Project Design



   64.      A focused approach to materialize the transformative impact of digital services in one sector

   only is more efficient than a broad approach across several verticals. A broad approach that would tackle

   the digital transformation of several sectors at once would spread out resources, complicate coordination,

   and likely produce fewer results. Comparable projects, such as the Safe Schooling and Distance Education

   Project (P173997) in Turkey and the Côte d’Ivoire E-Agriculture Project (P160418), have focused their

   efforts on one sector in addition to the foundational digital/ICT sector. Through Component 3, the

   proposed project focuses solely on the digitalization of the agricultural sector and aims to use this vertical

   as a proof of concept to later extend the intervention to other sectors that could benefit from digital

   transformation.



   65.    While focused in terms of socioeconomic sectors addressed, the approach still must be

   comprehensive on both the supply and demand sides. The project draws on the World Bank’s vast

   experience in digital infrastructure investments and telecom market reform, as well as on a growing body







                                                                                                          Page 42 of 92


The World Bank

Acceleration of the Digital Transformation of Cameroon Project (P173240)







   of industry research around factors that affect digital access.84 Building on an analysis of Cameroon’s

   broadband value chain, including gaps in the enabling environment and bottlenecks on the supply and

   demand sides, the project’s design reflects lessons learned from many other countries85 that point to the

   need for a comprehensive intervention that tackles all digital access barriers: the legal and regulatory

   framework, broadband connectivity, affordable mobile devices and data packages, digital literacy, and the

   availability of relevant content. Areas financed by the project such as device affordability will draw on

   research conducted with partners, such as GSMA, Facebook Connectivity, and A4AI; smartphone subsidy

   schemes used in Ghana, Columbia, and Malaysia;86 and asset-backed guarantee schemes for smartphones

   trialed in Argentina,87 Pakistan,88 and India.89



   66.      Digital inclusion should be fully embedded in the approach to ensure that the poorest and most

   marginalized benefit from digital services. Proactive interventions are needed to ensure that digital

   services are affordable and accessible to the poorest and most marginalized citizens to empower them

   with significant opportunities and benefits. Without such interventions, only those already at the top of

   the pyramid will benefit, exacerbating inequality. The project aims to expand access to rural areas and

   marginalized populations; lower the cost and increase the quality of internet services; and enable youth,

   women, and people with disabilities to benefit from entrepreneurship opportunities and digital skills

   training programs.



   67.      High-level political commitment and proper coordination are even more crucial when ambitious

   reforms and innovative approaches are undertaken. Given the scope of the project, the complexity of

   the design, the breadth of the proposed reforms, and the number of governmental agencies involved, it

   is crucial that strong political backing be secured at the highest levels and that a proper coordination

   mechanism be put in place to ensure efficient implementation. The project aims to fulfill these two

   conditions through a multitiered implementation arrangement (detailed in section III) that consists of a

   steering committee, a technical committee, a Project Coordination Unit, and ad hoc departmental

   committees. In addition, PBCs have been added to Component 1 to ensure reforms are implemented

   efficiently—a lesson drawn from other projects such as the Digital Transformation for User-Centric Public

   Services (P168425) in Tunisia.90 Finally, experiences show that ongoing training can improve awareness

   and reduce technical and administrative capacity gaps that hinder project implementation and that it is

   crucial to achieving project outcomes.



   68.       Public-sector funding or de-risking is needed to properly incentivize private telecom operators

   to invest in areas that would otherwise remain excluded due to low profitability. The project’s

   connectivity elements leverage lessons learned from a comparative analysis of over 70 last-mile

   connectivity deployments91 with respect to low-cost models and best practices to crowd in the private

   sector’s participation. Following the MFD approach, the project will seek to establish a PPP framework

   with competitive awards of capital subsidies to private telecom operators, a mechanism that was utilized

   successfully for rural connectivity investments in Tanzania and Niger. This tender mechanism ensures that

   public resources are utilized only to meet the minimum subsidy required for private-sector operators to

   roll out infrastructure and services in rural areas considered too risky or with an average revenue per user

   too low for a purely private investment.



   69.       Data-driven agriculture management information systems for digital agriculture are an

   important driver of improved public policy decisions. The project will support building digital data-driven

   agriculture management information systems focused on agropastoral statistics, cultivable soil systems,

   and livestock animal health. Experiences from other World Bank projects demonstrate improved policy

   decisions when such management information systems were used. For example, a World Bank-supported

   project in Uruguay92 ensured the protection of soil quality and 100 percent traceability of cattle through

   a national information system that monitored fertilizer application and by using another national system

   for livestock information that uses GPS-enabled chips as well as livestock producer registry. Another

   example of an efficient soil management system is EthioSIS, which uses remote sensing and satellite

   technology to create a digital map of the country’s soil. Based on these data, Ethiopia has revamped its

   fertilizer recommendations and farmers are applying tailored blends that are scientifically proven to

   provide the greatest yields in their specific geographies with the least environmental impact.93 Livestock

   and animal health management systems are emerging as a critical tool for public policy making, especially

   in the context of widespread animal epidemic outbreaks worldwide.



   70.     E-vouchers for farm input subsidies can lead to productivity gains. The proposed project will

    E.      Rationale for Bank Involvement and Role of Partners



   55.      From its global experience, the World Bank is well positioned to convene development partners

   and effectively leverage investment and technical assistance support incorporating the best practices. The

   scale of the challenges and the resources needed to transform Mozambique’s power sector and achieve

   universal access to electricity by 2030 calls for an integrated, long-term support program, well beyond the

   capacity of one institution. Coordinated, strategic, and well-sequenced donor support is critical to achieve

   scale and maximize added value. The World Bank is in a unique position to provide the needed expertise

   and the neutral advice, remain involved in the long term, and gain buy-in and support from the

   Government at the highest level. The World Bank supported the development of the NES in an extensive

   consultative process with power sector stakeholders and GoM authorities and has leveraged US$153

   million under ProEnergia in support of the Programa Nacional de Energia para Todos, and donors have

   expressed intent to continue support to the program.



   56.     The World Bank draws on its decades-long experience to support Mozambique in its endeavor to

   accelerate increased electricity access. The World Bank has supported on-grid and off-grid solution

   development in other Sub-Saharan African countries, including Zambia, (Electricity Service Access Project

   [P162760]), Niger (Electricity Access Expansion Project [P153743] and Niger Solar Electricity Access Project

   [P160170]), Ethiopia (Ethiopia Electrification Program [P160395]), and Kenya (Electricity Modernization

   Project [P120014] and Kenya Off-grid Solar Access Project for Underserved Counties [P160009]).



   57.      The World Bank is well positioned to support the GoM’s aspirations to bring universal coverage

   of digital services to its citizens. The World Bank has been supporting this agenda for several decades

   across the six global regions, including through investments under the MEGCIP39 which closed in 2017 and

   the Mozambique Digital Economy Diagnostic40 completed in 2019. The rural broadband and digital device

   affordability activities are intended as pilots for potential scale-up under the pipeline Mozambique Digital

   Acceleration Project (P176459) for delivery in FY23, which will aim to expand access to broadband for

   individuals, business, and government and to enable digital transformation in strategic economic and

   social sectors.



   58.      In the case of broadband, there is a strong rationale for public funding of the project, given the

   public goods nature of the benefits derived from the project and the potential to increase overall

   inclusion. While access to digital infrastructure has been considered important for some time, the

   emergence of the COVID-19 crisis has turned it into a necessity and has created the need to accelerate

   the rollout of the network in a major way and without further delay, partnering with the private sector as

   much as possible. By targeting underserved areas, the project would bring valuable economic and social

   benefits to a portion of the population of Mozambique, which would otherwise remain excluded without

   public intervention. This population is defined by low capita incomes, low average revenue per user, and

   limited private infrastructure and services offerings in low density and remote rural areas.

   National Energy for All Program. The Governments of Norway and Sweden have expressed interest in

    F.           Lessons Learned and Reflected in the Project Design



   61.     The project benefits from a long history of involvement of the World Bank, other donors, and the

   private sector in electricity and broadband access projects, including ongoing projects in Mozambique.

   Lessons learned to date from the implementation of ProEnergia will be incorporated in the design of the

   on-grid and off-grid electrification components. The following lessons have informed the project’s design:



               (a)    Electricity access expansion should be guided by a clear vision that is grounded on a least-

                      cost approach to electrification planning. The proposed project follows the Government’s

                      Programa Nacional de Energia para Todos launched in 2018. The Government strategy is

                      based on geospatial least-cost planning and integrates grid, mini grid, and off-grid

                      technologies with the goal to achieve universal electricity access by 2030. The project’s

                      design responds to the investment needs identified in the NES and investment decisions

                      follow geospatial least-cost analysis.

               (b)    Citizen engagement and stakeholder engagement are critical success factors for access to

                      clean energy and broadband services. For projects with direct impact at the household level,

                      mechanisms for obtaining regular feedback and enhance awareness have a direct bearing

                      on project outcomes. The proposed project therefore includes elements that focus on citizen

                      engagement including: (i) a clear communications campaign before new connections are

                      made, (ii) basic education and awareness creation on the use of electricity and clean cooking

                      solutions, and (iii) continued dialogue across Government agencies to sustain political

                      support.

           (c)   The financial health of utilities should be considered in all access programs to ensure reliable

                 and quality service provisions. The proposed project therefore seeks to balance the need for

                 access expansion with EDM’s financial sustainability by funding capital expenditure (CAPEX)

                 through grants and focusing on activities to improve the operational performance of EDM.

                 The expansion of broadband access under the proposed project also allows EDM access to

                 good-quality communication services to efficiently carry out its core activities for delivery of

                 electricity service to its customers.

           (d)   Bulk procurement of materials has yielded significant reductions in the cost of providing

                 electricity services. One of the new arrangements used for ProEnergia is the procurement of

                 the main materials in bulk, while the rest of materials are included as part of the installation

                 contracts. The first phase of procurement has resulted in an average reduction of 40 percent

                 in unit prices when compared with the projected prices and an overall saving of US$47

                 million. The proposed project will consider the same arrangements, but it will reduce the

                 materials purchased under this modality to the most advantageous to reduce procurement

                 times.

           (e)   Anchor loads in rural areas and prioritizing areas with medium-to-large-scale productive

                 uses of electricity increases sustainability. Therefore, prioritizing the electrification of target

                 areas based on potential demand from existing or planned agricultural loads to increase

                 productivity will help offset the service delivery and O&M cost recovery through tariffs and

                 could contribute to the sustainability of access programs (in particular, grid-based

                 electrification in peri-urban and rural areas).

           (f)   RBF has been demonstrated to be an effective approach to using public resources to

                 incentivize the market and can be designed to fit the country context and market conditions.

                 This has been proven effective in delivering solutions with predefined results in various

                 countries for both electricity and clean cooking solutions (for example, in Bangladesh, China,

                 Indonesia, Kenya, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Mongolia, and Uganda). These

                 mechanisms need to be accessible particularly to smaller enterprises to expand the depth

                 and reach of markets. The proposed project therefore combines RBF with grants, targeted

                 technical assistance to small enterprises, and credit enhancement support in a flexible

                 manner.

           (g)   The model used for expanding digital connectivity in rural areas has proven successful in the

                 region, including successful programs in Tanzania, Malawi, and Madagascar. The model

                 relies fully on the private sector for O&M, reducing sustainability concerns or further

                 financial liabilities for the Government. A ‘national roaming’ provision will be included for all

                 new infrastructure to allow subscribers of any mobile provider to connect to the towers at

                 no additional surcharge. This will allow retail level competition, prevent wasteful duplication

                 of infrastructure, and has been shown to stimulate user adoption more quickly, providing

                 greater benefits to the local community while also improving the economics of deployment

                 by stimulating greater revenue generating traffic.

                 reflect the fragility context. Appropriate quality product selection, distribution approaches,

                 training and full engagement of beneficiaries and stakeholders, in addition to proper

                 planning for risk mitigation, can help create effective safeguards to enhance project

C. Lessons Learned and Reflected in the Project Design

40. The project design incorporates lessons learned from the land sector in Côte d’Ivoire, including from

    previous IDA support, and addresses the drivers of land conflicts between indigenous land owners and

    migrant land users. The project will be implemented under a single implementing agency (AFOR) that is

    uniquely responsible for the entire land registration process, and the project will operate through AFOR

    rather than through a stand-alone PIU that is disconnected from the government’s program. The project will

    also introduce a number of innovations to address challenges faced by earlier projects, including a new

    clarification phase to provide a foundation for a more informed and participatory registration process; a new

    phase to register land use agreements through land leases between land uers and certificate holders; more

    inclusive CVGFRs that incorporate the perspectives of all social groups, including migrants; and a simplified

    village boundary demarcation process that will remove the costly and politically-contentious process of

    registering village boundaries.

41. More broadly, the project design incorporates numerous lessons learned from recent and on-going

    systematic rural land registration processes in Côte d’Ivoire and the region, as described below:

           a) Fit-for-purpose: The low overall rate of land registration in the region, including in Côte d’Ivoire,

              highlights the need to design participatory registration procedures using simple technologies that

              are affordable for local landholders and that provide a level of tenure security and accuracy

              commensurate with existing demand. Rural land tenure in Côte d’Ivoire remains largely governed

              by customary practice and varies across the country. While individual land certificates may be

              appropriate in the west and southeast, where a history of relatively intensive cash cropping has

              led rights to be relatively individualized, collective certification is more likely to be appropriate in

              the center and north, where group ownership of land remains the norm. Moreover, while sub-

              meter accuracy standards may be appropriate in more peri-urban rural areas, where land values

              are generally higher and land markets are already emerging, experience from Ethiopia,

              Madagascar and even densely-populated Rwanda suggests that highly accurate fixed boundaries

              are less important than general boundaries that are acknowledged by the local community and

              the government for low value rural lands with relatively limited land market activity. The project

              will therefore adopt a participatory and cost-effective certification process that builds on local

              knowledge of existing land rights, involves community members in land certification, uses simple

              and modern technologies, and will be tested through a small-scale pilot to build local ownership

              and awareness and ensure the procedures align with existing capacity and customary land tenure

              practices.

           b) Develop and then test a low-cost, participatory, and systematic land registration process: The

              project will support the development of a systematic land registration process that uses best

              practices for low-cost and participatory first time land registration that build on the pilot

              experience of a non-profit organization, Institut Audace Afrique. These include the use of cost-

              effective digital technologies for mapping and registering land rights, such as high resolution

              satellite imagery, mobile phones/tablets; the inclusion of neighboring land holders, customary





                                                                                                                Page 23 of 120


The World Bank

Cote d'Ivoire Land Policy Improvement and Implementation Project (P157206)







           authorities, and neighboring village representatives in the registration process; and the use of

           local para-surveyors and para-archivists to support participatory village and parcel mapping. In

           addition, the project will provide technical assistance to the DFR and the Working Group to make

           the necessary regulatory revisions to facilitate this new systematic registration process, as well as

           simplifications to the existing sporadic registration procedures, and to ensure their compatibility.

           Finally, this first project will pilot test these new procedures in one or two regions initially and

           eventually in selected areas of a limited number of additional regions and support additional

           procedural and regulatory revisions as needed through an adaptive process that will ultimately

           lay the foundation for scaling up systematic land registration in the second project.

      c) Formally document all forms of customary land rights: While the Rural Land Law provides for the

         formal recognition of customary land ownership rights through land certificates, the project has

         been explicitly designed to result in formal documentation of all land rights holders (“a paper for

         everyone” / “un papier pour tous”), regardless of the nature of these rights (e.g., ownership,

         access, use), given the well-recognized multiplicity of land rights within the region. The need to

         document land use and access rights is especially important in the context of Côte d’Ivoire, where

         women’s customary land rights remain relatively weak and disputes over land access between

         autochthone land owners and migrant land users contributed to the civil conflict. The project will

         thus incorporate recent innovative approaches to scan and archive petits papiers and will

         furthermore support the formalization of these land contracts.

      d) Inclusive: In addition to women and migrants, youth also often face difficulty accessing and

         maintaining control over land that is important for their livelihoods. Pastoral herders also need

         temporary transit rights through farmlands to access critical water and grazing points. As such,

         the project includes targeted citizen engagement and communications activities to raise

         awareness of the value of securing and strengthening the rights of women, migrants, and youth

         and of formalizing the customary land access arrangements negotiated between farmers and

         herders. These activities will be critical given that previous efforts to formalize customary land

         rights in Africa have been accused of excluding and further marginalizing women and other

         vulnerable groups whose land rights may be secondary to those of the dominant group.13

      e) Streamlined and long-term land administration: Secure land tenure ultimately depends on

         effective land administration, which itself depends not only on the capacity of local authorities to

         manage and update land registry databases, but also on landholder demand for land services,

         including to register changes in land ownership or use rights. In contexts where customary or

         informal governance of land continues to predominate rural land administration, as in Côte

         d’Ivoire, experience – for example from Cambodia, Ethiopia, and Rwanda – suggests that land

         administration systems need to be designed not only for massive first-time land registration, but

         also to allow for subsequent changes in land rights to easily be registered at low cost and with a

         minimum number of steps and institutions involved. The experience of Rwanda, where the

         government achieved an impressive scale of first-time land registration but land transactions

         remain largely informal, highlights the need to raise awareness of and demand for maintaining

         formal records of land ownership as transactions inevitably occur. The reformed institutional

         structure and land registration procedures that will be supported by the project will streamline

          rural land registration and administration under AFOR to facilitate easy and affordable

          registration of subsequent transactions in local land registries and the national SIF. The project

          will also include public communications campaigns about the importance of formally registering

          changes in land rights and engage citizens to better understand their concerns with and

          constraints to registration to ensure that the land registry continues to reflect existing realities on

          the ground. This will be particularly important to achieve the program’s overall goal of formalizing

          the active informal rural land market in Côte d’Ivoire to reduce an important source of land

          conflicts and to ensure that user fees provide sustainable financing for rural land administration.

     f)   Capacity building: Previous land policy implementation efforts in the region have stalled as a

          result of limited capacity within government and among private sector service providers, such as

          surveyors. As such, the project includes an explicit and substantial training component

          (Component 3) to build a new generation of professionals, from technicians to engineers. The

          project will also support short courses and on-the-job training for existing land professionals to

          facilitate their implementation of the new legal and regulatory framework for rural land tenure.

     g) Citizen engagement, conflict prevention, and conflict mediation: Given the potential for land

        rights formalization to bring previously latent land conflicts to the fore, the project will

        incorporate various kinds of conflict prevention and mediation support involving local customary

        and formal authorities depending on the nature of the dispute. These activities will be tailored to

        the local socio-cultural and political economy context based on the outcomes of the Social

        Assessment. Previous land registration processes in Côte d’Ivoire have in many cases been

        delayed due to misunderstandings over whose rights can be recognized, the implications of the

        procedures (for example, that village boundary demarcation does not confer ownership rights,

        and members of one village can certify their parcels within another village), and village boundary

        disputes. The project will therefore add a new clarification step to land registration that seeks to

        proactively engage citizens in a participatory rights identification exercise and increase their

        understanding of the relevant laws and procedures. The revised land registration procedures will

        also register land use agreements, mitigating a key concern of land users that the land certification

        process will undermine their existing land use rights. To ensure that disputed parcels or village

        boundaries do not indefinitely delay registration of agreed boundaries, alternative dispute

        resolution mechanisms will be supported through customary community leaders and local

        government authorities (e.g., prefect, sub-prefect) where land owners or villages cannot agree on

        a shared boundary. Also, importantly, resources will be reserved to return to the conflict-affected

        areas to complete the registration process once the dispute has been resolved.

     h) Client ownership and donor coordination: Learning from previous IDA and donor support to rural

        development in Côte d’Ivoire, including the Rural Land Management and Community

        Infrastructure Development Project, the IDA finance will be executed through existing

        Government institutions with support from private technical operators and the participation of

        local community members, and all sector donors have agreed to align their support with the

        Government’s National Land Rural Land Tenure Security Program. Finance from the IDA and other

        donors will thus directly support the national and decentralized public institutions charged with

        rural land policy and administration, including the DFR and the newly established AFOR at the

        national level and the CVGFR at the village level. This will avoid the coordination and sustainability

        challenges associated with multiple stand-alone project implementation units and ensure close

        cooperation and buy-in from the relevant Government institutions throughout implementation,

                  while building Government capacity for sustainability after external financing ends. Program

                  preparation involved all relevant Government agencies, as well as donors, private technical

                  operators, and NGOs active in the sector and also private citizens. Furthermore, implementation

                  will be coordinated under a single ministry to ensure close alignment of activities managed by

                  different executing agencies and avoid an onerous multi-ministerial coordination unit. To further

                  strengthen existing Government institutions and streamline implementation, the AFOR Steering

IV. IMPLEMENTATION



A. Institutional and Implementation Arrangements



 42. To ensure sustainability and build AFOR’s capacity to serve as the com prehensive implementing agency

     for the 1998 Rural Land Law, the IDA finance will be managed by AFOR using competitively-selected staff.14

     The Government is implementing the PNSFR through a program approach. In accordance with the decree

     creating AFOR and following the needed regulatory reforms, implementation of rural land registration will

     now be streamlined under AFOR to promote coherent, coordinated, and standardized approaches for land

     registration nationwide. Since the 2016 decree that established AFOR provides it with full responsibility to

     manage public funding, the IDA financing will be managed directly by AFOR rather than through a separate

     Project Implementation Unit to ensure that PNFSR implementation is streamlined under a single national

     institution. Other donors have also expressed their interest in directly financing AFOR to avoid a proliferation

     of Project Implementation Units and procedures. To fulfill its mandate, AFOR must oversee the

     implementation of a single program of land activities throughout rural Côte d’Ivoire in compliance with a

     single comprehensive Field Operations Manual that will be developed under the project. Also with support

     from the IDA financing, AFOR will develop a single monitoring and evaluation system and a single reporting

     system as part of a single comprehensive Project Implementation Manual. As long as the AFOR Director and

     Deputy Director continue to be financed through public funds, they will be eligible to authorize expenditures

     in accordance with the World Bank policies and procedures.

 43. In accordance with the 2005 Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness, the Government of Côte d’Ivoire

     requested close coordination among the donors supporting the rural land sector. To avoid inconsistencies in

     procedures and implementation and the duplication of reporting and M&E systems, AFOR will have a single

     set of policies and procedures that are acceptable to the IDA and other donors to the sector. As AFOR is a

     new institution whose effective establishment currently depends on the IDA finance, the operational and

     procedural manuals, as well as the safeguards norms, will be aligned with IDA requirements. Thus, AFOR will

     be considered as the project implementation unit (PIU) of the IDA financing. AFOR will be responsible for

     procuring all goods and services under this project for all implementing partners and for providing overall

     monitoring and management of the use of the IDA finance. To overcome the registration implementation

     challenges identified above, AFOR will be responsible for overseeing the overall implementation of the new

     4-in-1 systematic land registration process. AFOR will procure, monitor, and evaluate qualified

     multidisciplinary private service providers (OTA), who will conduct all of the field work, prepare the

     certification applications and improved contracts, and submit all documentation to AFOR. The Préfet will

     remain responsible for final validation and signature of all land certificates. To avoid gaps or inconsistencies

 Box 4: Towards an e-KYC (Know-Your-Customer) registry



 To facilitate the opening of accounts in financial institutions for financially excluded populations, this digital

 data platform will host an e-KYC (Know-Your-Customer) registry. The registry will help financial institutions to

 identify their customers and comply with Customer Due Diligence (CDD) regulation which constitute a key

      The World Bank

component for compliance with AML/CFT requirements. Indeed, high costs incurred by complex and time-

consuming KYC controls and diligences are often considered as main barriers to financial inclusion. These costs

are likely to keep financial institutions from providing financial services to the disadvantaged population which

may not be considered sufficiently profitable. Recognizing this critical issue, the G20 High Level Principles on

Digital Financial Inclusion issued by the Global Partnership for Financial Inclusion (GPFI) in 2016 included the

need to facilitate customer ID for digital financial services as a key pillar for financial inclusion under its principle

7.



The e-KYC platform intends to help authorities of Niger to comply with this principle, by designing and providing

an e-KYC registry which will facilitate the ID process of customers (whether permanent of occasional, and

whether natural or legal person), the verification of customer’s identity, and the implementation of on-going

customer monitoring.



In addition, supervisors will also take benefit of the information stored in the e-KYC registry which may facilitate

their controls (on documentary fraud or suspicious activity reports for instance). This registry could lead the

supervisors to adjust their internal procedures in terms of controls and propose legal amendments to the

AML/CFT law if necessary, contributing therein to the implementation of an effective AML/CFT risk-based

supervisory approach.



From a technical point of view, this e-KYC registry may take different forms and will have to be adapted to the

Nigerien context after considering the main conclusions issued by the WBG Policy Note on e-KYC registries that

is currently being finalized, as well as knowledge about all potential tools existing on the market. However, as

potential characteristics (provided below only as examples and close to the Indian model), the e-KYC registry

could enable new clients to submit directly on the digital platform a dully filled and signed KYC form (with

supporting documents to verify proof of identity and proof of address and potentially linked to digital ID) before

being allotted via SMS or email a single digit KYC ID number (KIN) which would need to be quoted by the client

while conducting any financial transaction. For existing clients, financial institutions could be able to submit

directly on the platform the required documents using bulk upload or file transfer mechanisms. The technical

modalities of access of the e-KYC registry by the financial institutions will have to be determined by the

technological solutions’ provider.



The e-KYC registry will be applicable in the first place only to individuals (population of Smart Villages) but could

be extended to the entire population of Niger in the medium term. The authorities will have to define the

business model of the e-KYC registry, as to whether it should be financially sustainable (charging fees for

financial institutions or/and administrative or judicial authorities to access the data) or encourage financial

                                          ANNEX 2: Economic and Financial Analysis



1. The scope of the connectivity activity in Component 2 (i.e. extending digital connectivity to targeted rural areas)

   involves the construction of a digital infrastructure in the rural and remote parts of Niger to cover the targeted

   villages. According to the ANSI, there are around 500,000 inhabitants in the 2,111 targeted villages that are not

   covered by any mobile signal. The construction of the digital infrastructure will allow for an important expansion in

   the provision of mobile telephony services and mobile broadband services to citizens and smallholders. This is

   particularly crucial in closing the gender gap in mobile phone ownership/ usage, where women are not covered by

   mobile signal in their home/village but are not allowed to leave it.

2. The financial and economic analysis of the project is based on the incremental approach37. All cash flows are stated

   in constant US$. The reference period is set equal to the standard lifecycle period for a digital infrastructure (i.e. 20

   years) and thus no residual value is considered at the end of the reference period.



3. Component 2 – The project is viable financially and economically

     a. The results for the project without public capital support are: (i) the Financial Rate of Return FRR(C) is 7 percent;

        (ii) the break-even point occurs in 15 years; and (iii) the NPV is -US$22.7 million (with a discount rate of 10

        percent). These results show that although FRR(C) is positive, telecommunication operators would not invest in

        this project alone because it would not provide the minimum rate of return that private mobile operator

        companies usually expect (around 12 to 16 percent depending on the socio-economic context). Therefore, public

        Government financing is needed to make the project possible.

     b. The results for the project with public capital support are: (i) the Financial Rate of Return FRR(K) is 14 percent;

        (ii) the break-even point occurs in 12 years; and (iii) the Net Present Value NPV(K) is US$23.8 million (with a

        discount rate of 10 percent). These results show that the project becomes acceptable for private operators.

        Moreover, the fact that after taking into account the public capital, the Financial Rate of Return FRR(K) is in the

        average of the expected rate of return for standard mobile telecommunications projects and that the break-

        even point occurs in the long-term (12 years) show that the public capital support is not over-proportionate.

     c. Although last-mile operators were consulted in advance, there is a high level of uncertainty with regards to the

        revenues that will be generated by the infrastructure. This is acknowledged in the design of the project, which

        requires the inclusion of a claw-back mechanism into the PPP contract that would apply in case revenues are

        higher than originally foreseen.

     d. A sensitivity analysis is performed on the assumptions for the supply-side (unit cost of a site and OPEX as a

        percentage rate of CAPEX), the demand-side (penetration rate and ARPU), and the discount factor. It shows that

        the business model is sensitive to the assumptions and could be overly profitable, thus reinforcing the need of a

        claw-back mechanism.

     e. The economic analysis can be performed on a macroeconomic level (estimate the local GDP growth generated

        by additional mobile and broadband users) or a microeconomic level (such as household consumer surplus or

        time and cost savings derived from the use of online services). However, the economic analysis cannot be

        performed by using these methods due to: (i) the coverage expansion areas (white zones) being scattered rather

(i) Demand led capacity development through training. A diversified pool of public,

    private and non-governmental organization (NGO) training providers will be used to

    environmental and natural resources concerns and constraints, and promoting sound

    sustainability, financial management, climate adaptation, nutrition, and social and

    gender implications. A prominent feature of this sub-component is the design and

    delivery of training by Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs), involving farmers,

    agribusiness companies, and training institutions. Capacity building needs and

    activities would be identified under sub-component 1.1 by value chain actors

    themselves. In designing and conducting the training, challenges and priorities

    expressed by women farmers will be taken into account. This may include involving

    women farmers in climate-smart trials and demonstrations, and the development of

    training curricula. Similarly, where relevant, training activities will aim to provide the

    youth with livelihood options and skills that would enable them to respond to

    employment opportunities along the value chain.

   Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) aims to achieve climate change adaptation, mitigation and food security, increasing

crop productivity and resilience. The adoption of climate-smart agriculture practices, such as conservation agriculture,

no tillage systems, crop diversification and intercropping, improved water management, crop residue mulching,

improved seeds, agroforestry can support them to increase and sustain crop productivity for their commercial

production as well as subsistence production and produce environmental benefits such as increasing soil moisture and

reducing land degradation. Local studies have shown positive impacts of CSA practices: within 4-5 years, degraded

soils can be restored by climate-smart agriculture practice such as conservation agriculture, agroforestry, afforestation;

adoption of conservation agriculture over a 5 year rotation can lead to a 66 percent increase of crop yields per year for

rice and maize.

   43.      This subcomponent aims to enhance the competitiveness of Ivorian farmers and enterprises in

   supported value chains by financing investment mechanisms that will provide common services and

   productive assets currently missing but needed to increase quality standards, add value to products,

   and access higher value-added markets. Operationalizing GVCs requires an integral and comprehensive

   approach that addresses all market failures along the value chain. The supported value chains face market

   failures such as coordination failures (primarily), information asymmetries, underdevelopment of public

   goods (including club goods), and negative externalities. The CRIs will identify the market failures affecting

   the supported value chains and propose the policy reforms and common services required to overcome

   them. Most commonly, these services would be club goods28 that require economies of scale. The

   investments in this component will be aligned with the following principles: (a) follow a Maximizing

   Finance for Development (MFD) approach: when feasible, the common services will be delivered by the

   private sector and (b) create the least market distortions (for example, long-term subsidies, monopsonies,

   and so on). An example of some coordination failures in the mango value chain are presented in Box 2.



   44.     This subcomponent will finance two investment mechanisms and digital solutions. The

   investment mechanisms are (a) Matching Grants for Common Services and (b) Provision or construction

   of Common Productive Assets, with Matching Grants. In this operation, common services and common

   productive assets differ based on whether service providers are currently able to provide the services

   proposed by the CRIs or not. The Matching Grants for Common Services are for common services where

   service providers already exist in the market. Mechanism 2 is designed to provide (that is, construct, buy)

   new, common productive assets for which there are no private operators capable of providing the service

   due to high upfront costs of setting up the assets or services. The investment mechanisms will use digital

   solutions (for example, blockchain) for all supported value chains, for traceability, quality control, and

   accounting purposes. Some value chains may require the use of both investment mechanisms.









   28 Club goods are a sub-type of public goods that are excludable but non-rivalrous—that is, it is not diminished as access is

   broadened, but users can be prevented from accessing it. Classic examples of club goods are cinemas, private parks, or satellite

   television. In the context of industrial development, club goods are often underprovided. This happens for two reasons: (a) it is

   difficult to enforce the exclusion of non-payers (and hence the club good becomes a public good, with problems of ‘free riding’)

   or (b) individuals cannot coordinate among themselves to finance the provision of the club good or club service.

     Box 2. Examples of Coordination Market Failures in the Mango Value Chain and Early Results for Piloting

     Value Chain Blockchain Solution in Haiti

     With an annual production of around 150,000 tons, of which 32,000 tons are exported per year, Côte d'Ivoire is

     the leading exporter of mangoes in Africa and the second supplier to the European market. Mango is the third

     most exported fruit from Côte d'Ivoire, after banana and pineapple. The primary mango season extends from

     January through May and the mango sector includes approximately 7,000 actors. The main stakeholders are (a)

     producers; (b) exporters with their own conditioning facilities; (c) processors; (d) private companies (input

     suppliers, box suppliers, post-harvest infrastructure, and loading operation at the fruit terminal at the port); and

     (e) research centers. Available data reveal that a case of mangoes (30 mangoes) sold for CFAF 1,478 (US$2.71) in

     2012 and CFAF 1,012 (US$1.86)—or US$0.06 cents per mango—in 2013, at farmgate. Farmers’ revenues

     fluctuated around CFAF 130,950 (US$240) between the 2011 and 2013 seasons.

     Mangoes in the European market sell for approximately US$2 per kg (approximately US$2 for two mangoes). To

     increase farmers’ revenues, a series of coordination failures need to be addressed to sell directly to the European

     market. For example, mangoes need hot-water treatment to control for fruit fly larvae, their temperature needs

     to be quickly lowered to around 12°C and they require temperature-controlled logistics within a few hours after

     treatment to ensure longer shelf life until destination, where the mangoes can ripen. Despite the presence of

     logistic services in Côte d’Ivoire, the mango farmers are not organized nor have access to the financing required

     to coordinate the value chain services to access these export market. On the financing side, the farmers require

     supply chain financing rather than other types of loans. In particular, they need short-term advances that use the

     product—that is, the mangoes kept under strict quality control—as the collateral.

     A public blockchain solution for value chains was recently piloted in the Haiti Business Development and

     Investment Project (P123974). To increase the incomes of fresh fruit producers, especially mango farmers, the

     project connected producers in Haiti to consumers in the North American market. Beyond enabling the sale of

     mangoes in the international market, the project has supported the training of producers in proper harvesting

     techniques, and transport and cold chain management, which can optimize post-harvest yields. The project set

     up a cold chain logistics service in key producing regions of the country to sell fresh fruit to the United States and

     strengthen the competitiveness of Haiti’s fresh fruit sector. Connecting producers to this key market has t he

     potential to raise them out of poverty and increase overall economic resilience. As a result of the project’s CRIs,

     use of the blockchain solution and provision of third-party temperature-controlled logistics providers, in 2020, 58

     mango farmers involved in the project exported directly, without intermediaries, nearly 52,000 pounds of

     mangoes to the United States. These sales generated over 238 percent higher income than if these mangoes were

     sold on the local market. The project closes in 2021 and has also expanded to specialty coffee, fine cacao, and

     avocado to the United States using the same system.

   45.      The economic rationale of these Matching Grants is to support eligible beneficiaries (farmers

   and firms) to meet new quality standards, primarily for the EU or US markets, through common services

   required to compete in more attractive markets. In particular, these Matching Grants are designed to

   correct coordination failures faced by farmers and firms in supported value chains by providing the

   common services that are currently missing (and for which service providers already exist in the market

   but are not providing the service to a particular area or group due to coordination failures). Under this

   mechanism, the PCU would competitively select service providers based on studies, technical

   specifications, or SOPs developed under Subcomponent 1.1.



   46.     The Matching Grants for Common Services are an innovative instrument which would finance

   advance payments of eligible expenses. Examples of eligible expenses include the following types of

   services: postharvest temperature-controlled or other specialized logistics service, collection points,

   brokerage services, packaging facilities, harvest planning or maturity mapping services29, international

   shipping/export, technical assistance and training (for example, dissemination of quality certification and

   standardization initiatives and middle management training), and/or a combination of these services. To

   address coordination failure(s), advances are needed to make the service available to the cluster actors;

   however, to control for the risk of abuse of advance payment of eligible expenses, a set of eligibility

   conditions must be met to activate the mechanism. These include (a) pre-registration of beneficiaries; (b)

   meeting of quality standards defined by SOPs or other specifications and ensuring quality control provided

   by a third-party service provider; (c) use of the blockchain solution by the service provider to schedule

   pickups, ensure quality control, consolidate small lots into larger batches for export, and so on; and (d)

   use of an escrow account to manage advances and payments based on instructions received from the

   blockchain solution.30



   47.     By combining the matching grant advances with the eligibility conditions above, the funds will

   be replenished into an escrow account to be reinvested in more common services in the supported

   value chains. The key principle of any of the supported export initiatives is that the products will be

   competitive and will not need any subsidy to cover any of the extra costs involved. However, the Matching

   Grant mechanism needs to provide funds to allow the farmers and service providers to engage and export.

   Once the products are exported, sold, and the profits received, the beneficiaries will be ready to save for

   future reinvestment of the subsidy received as a Matching Grant. To reinforce future reinvestments, the

   PCU will open a Joint Savings Account for the beneficiaries which would allow the beneficiaries to finance

   future common services. Eligible common services for investment by the beneficiaries would include any

   common service that would support production, harvest, or post-harvest activities of the cluster. The

   modalities and rules relative to the Joint Savings Account will be further defined in the Matching Grants

   Manual. In total, it is expected that the Matching Grants for Common Services will support an estimated

   3,000 farmers and 100 firms and allow for an average value of advances of US$7,000 per beneficiary.

   partnership with a commercial bank. This third party will manage the escrow accounts through the
